summary: Defines a structure by which information servers exchange indices from their databases in the Common Indexing Protocol, along with the meanings of its headers. It is experimental.

plainLanguage.summary: Search engines that sit on different databases can cooperate if they share a summary of what they hold. RFC 2654 defines that summary as a tagged index object: a list of values where each value carries the number of the record it belongs to. Because the numbers travel with the values, a server can send only what has changed since last time instead of the whole index again.

questions: how do servers exchange directory indexes
what is cip common indexing protocol
subtitle: A compact index format that lets search servers share what they hold without resending everything.

tldr.problem: Search servers that hold different parts of one large directory need to exchange summaries of their contents, so that a query can be sent to the server most likely to hold the answer.
tldr.mechanism: The tagged index object attaches identification numbers to data values, so values carrying the same number belong to the same record. It supports a full index and incremental updates built from add, delete and update blocks.
tldr.outcome: A server can send only what changed since the last exchange, which matters for servers holding millions of records. The document is Experimental.

today: RFC 2654 is an Experimental document and has not been obsoleted or updated. It is one part of a set: the index object format defined here is designed to be carried by the Common Indexing Protocol described in RFC 2651, alongside the index-mesh work in RFC 2657.

sections.title: The Common Indexing Protocol and the Index Object
sections.content:
The Common Indexing Protocol (CIP), described in RFC 2651, proposes a mechanism for distributing searches across several instances of a single type of search engine in order to create a global directory. It offers a scalable and flexible way to tie individual databases into distributed data warehouses that grow with the Internet, and it does this independently of whatever access method is used to reach the data behind the indices.

CIP itself does not say what an index object looks like. One index object already existed: the Centroid, derived from the Whois++ protocol. This memo defines a second one, the Tagged Index Object.

The Centroid does not meet all the requirements for exchanging index information between servers. It does not support incremental updates natively, and for a server holding millions of records, constantly exchanging complete copies of the database is expensive in bandwidth. The Tagged Index Object is built specifically to carry index updates, at the cost of a larger index object. It also labels each piece of information with an identifier that ties the individual attributes back to a record as a whole, which lets an index server direct a specific query to the server most likely to hold the answer.
sections.plainLanguage: The Common Indexing Protocol lets several search servers share the work of one big directory. This memo defines what one such server sends to another: an index object that ties each value to the record it came from, so a server can send only what changed since last time. The price is a larger message.

sections.title: Why Directories Need to Point at Each Other
sections.content:
LDAP gives access to information arranged hierarchically so as to provide a globally distributed database, called the Directory Information Tree (DIT). Several servers cooperate to manage a common subtree of it. The server responsible for the United States part of the tree must still answer a search about the Swedish part, and the normal answer is a referral to another server that is expected to know that subtree. No mechanism, though, lets the United States server point the client at the server that actually holds the Swedish records. An LDAP (v3) server is typically configured with the name of exactly one other LDAP server to which all clients are referred when their requests fall outside its own subtree.

The X.500 series defines the Directory Information Shadowing Protocol (DISP), which lets X.500 directory system agents exchange information about the tree. Shadowing is designed around exchanging entire portions of the tree. CIP and the Tagged Index Object are designed around exchanging structural index information about the tree instead, which improves the speed of navigating it. The memo argues that DISP is the better fit for spreading data and for fault tolerance, while the Tagged Index Object is the better fit for index exchange, and that it works outside X.500 as well.

Shadowing also needs an agreement: before it can occur, an agreement covering the conditions under which it may occur is required. Collecting meaningful replicas of a large part of the tree also needs a large database. The memo notes that the data in the tree is being exchanged between directory system agents rather than only the information needed to maintain an index, and that in many environments such an agreement is not the right shape.
sections.plainLanguage: Directory servers split one big tree of records between themselves. When a query lands on the wrong server, the usual answer is a referral, but that server can only name one other server to try. Sharing a summary of what each server holds would let it send the client straight to the right one.

sections.title: The Agreement Between the Two Servers
sections.content:
Before an object can be exchanged, the organisation administering the supplier and the organisation administering the consumer must reach an agreement. It names the index type, x-tagged-index-1, and gives an object identifier for the subtree and scope the index covers. It also sets a base URI for any referrals the index produces, the supplier's host name and listening port number, and a mailto: URI where the consumer can be reached. Later versions of the agreement allow other forms of URI, so the consumer may retrieve the update over the web, FTP or CIP instead.

The agreement also states how often the supplier produces updates. The update interval is the maximum duration in seconds between update occurrences. If the consumer has waited that long without an update since the previous one, its index information is likely out of date. A typical value for a server with frequent updates is 604800 seconds, or every week, while a server whose directory is modified only annually could use a much longer interval.

Two more fields decide how the data is shaped. The attribute namespace records which attribute names the group of servers has agreed to use and how local names map onto them. The consistency base decides how consistency is maintained across incremental updates: complete, which any server wanting to comply with the standard must support, or the optional tag and unique methods. A final field, the security option, chooses whether the update is sent in plaintext or signed and encrypted using PGP/MIME, S/MIME, SSLv3 or Fortezza.
sections.plainLanguage: Two servers that plan to exchange indexes first agree on a set of settings: which kind of index it is, where the data lives, how often updates arrive and how the data is protected. These settings travel with every update so that the receiving server knows how to read it.

sections.title: The Tagged Index Object Format
sections.content:
The update is a MIME object of type application/cip-index-object, with parameters for the type (application/index.obj.tagged), the object identifier and the base URI. The payload is mostly textual but may include bytes with the high bit set, so the sending server sets the content transfer encoding to suit the payload. The object may be encapsulated in a wrapper such as multipart/signed, or encrypted as part of the security procedure, and the result can be distributed by electronic mail. The payload is a series of CRLF-terminated lines in UTF-8. Some suppliers can only generate the printable US-ASCII subset, but every consumer must be able to handle the whole range of Unicode characters when decoding attribute values.

The grammar is given in modified BNF. An object is a sequence of parts; each part has a header, a schema specification and index information. The schema specification names each attribute and its token type. The index information is either a full index or an incremental one made of add, delete and update blocks. Every index line has the shape of an attribute name, a colon, a tag list, a slash and the value, and a value too long for one line continues on following lines that begin with a hyphen.

The header lines are: version, always present, holding x-tagged-index-1; updatetype, always present, either total or incremental, with the first update sent for a given subtree required to be total; thisupdate, always present, giving the number of seconds since 00:00:00 UTC January 1, 1970 at which the supplier built the update; lastupdate, present when the update type is incremental, so the consumer can tell whether it missed one; and contextsize, optional and supplied for statistical purposes only.

The token type says how a value is split into pieces for searching. FULL uses no delimiters. TOKEN splits on white space and the at sign. RFC822 also splits on the full stop. UUCP splits on white space and the exclamation mark. DNS splits on any character that is not a number, a letter or a hyphen.
sections.plainLanguage: The update is a MIME object holding lines of text. Each line names an attribute, lists the records the value belongs to, and gives the value itself. The header at the top says whether the object replaces the whole index or only carries changes, and when it was made.

sections.title: Incremental Updates
sections.content:
An incremental update carries only the changes made since the object named in the lastupdate header was distributed. If the receiving server never received that object, it should ask for a total index object instead. The changes arrive in three kinds of block: add, delete and update.

An Add Block holds lines for records that are new. They are guaranteed not to have existed in any tagged index object the receiver has already received, so the receiver can insert this information into the index it already keeps for the transmitting server. A Delete Block and an Update Block depend on the consistency method in force. With complete, a delete carries every token connected to the record, and an update carries both the old and the new versions of it. With tag, a delete carries the record's tokens under the tag it had in the last full update, and an update carries only the tokens that changed, in both their old and new forms. With unique, a delete carries only the unique identifier, and an update carries that identifier together with the tokens that changed.

An Update Block also lets a supplier start indexing an attribute it had not included before: it can send the index information on postal addresses for all its records and say that nothing else has changed. Tags are applied per entry, so two index lines with the same tag always refer to the same record and two with different tags refer to different records, and a star in the tag position means that token appears in every record in the directory. The tag a record carries in one full index may differ in the next, so receiving servers should make no assumptions about tag values across index object boundaries. Updates to an index based on tagged index objects must be performed in the order the object itself specifies.
sections.plainLanguage: An incremental update sends three kinds of change: records added, records deleted and records changed. How much each block has to carry depends on the method the two servers agreed on. The receiver applies the updates in the order the object gives them.

sections.title: Security and Privacy
sections.content:
This protocol transfers information between two servers, and that information may be protected by laws in many countries, so the methods used to tokenize the data have to be chosen with care, to make sure protected data cannot be reconstructed in full by the receiving server. The protocol has no inherent protection against spoofing or eavesdropping. Because it is transported inside MIME messages, as all CIP index objects are, it inherits all the security capabilities and liabilities of other MIME messages.

Information server administrators must decide what portions of their databases are appropriate for inclusion in the index object. For distribution of information outside the enterprise, the memo encourages facilities that hide the organisational structure when the object is generated from the underlying database.

To transmit index objects across the Internet, index servers should use SSL when completing the connection. To strongly verify the identity of the peer on the other side, the SSL version 3 certificate exchange should be implemented and the identity in the peer's certificate verified with the Public Key Infrastructure. If electronic mail is used to exchange the objects, then a secure messaging facility such as PGP/MIME or S/MIME should be used to sign or encrypt the information, or both.
sections.plainLanguage: The index can reveal what a server holds, so the two sides must protect it. The memo asks servers to encrypt the connection, to sign or encrypt the message when it travels by mail, and to choose how values are split so that the receiver cannot rebuild protected data.

viz.caption: THE TAGGED INDEX OBJECT GRAMMAR (RFC 2654 SECTION 4.3)

data.title: Modified BNF
data.code:
index-object = 0*(io-part SEP) io-part
io-part      = header SEP schema-spec SEP index-info
header       = version-spec SEP update-type SEP this-update SEP
               last-update context-size name-space SEP
version-spec = "version:" *SPACE "x-tagged-index-1"
update-type  = "updatetype:" *SPACE ( "total" |
               ( "incremental" [*SPACE "tagbased"|"uniqueIDbased" ] )
this-update  = "thisupdate:" *SPACE TIMESTAMP
last-update  = [ "lastupdate:" *SPACE TIMESTAMP SEP]
context-size = [ "contextsize:" *SPACE 1*DIGIT SEP]
schema-spec  = "BEGIN IO-Schema" SEP 1*(schema-line SEP)
               "END IO-Schema"
schema-line  = attribute-name ":" token-type
token-type   = "FULL" | "TOKEN" | "RFC822" | "UUCP" | "DNS"
index-info   = full-index | incremental-index
full-index   = "BEGIN Index-Info" SEP 1*(index-block SEP)
               "END Index-Info"
incremental-index = 1*(add-block | delete-block | update-block)
add-block    = "BEGIN Add Block" SEP 1*(index-block SEP)
               "END Add Block"
delete-block = "BEGIN Delete Block" SEP 1*(index-block SEP)
               "END Delete Block"
update-block = "BEGIN Update Block" SEP
               0*(old-index-block SEP)
               1*(new-index-block SEP)
               "END Update Block"
index-block  = first-line 0*(SEP cont-line)
first-line   = attr-name ":" *SPACE taglist "/" attr-value
cont-line    = "-" taglist "/" attr-value
taglist      = tag 0*("," tag) | "*"
tag          = 1*DIGIT ["-" 1*DIGIT]
attr-value   = 1*(UTF8)
